parts.text:
**Body Mass Index (BMI)** is a quick and simple screening tool used to estimate body fat based on a person's height and weight. 

While it is widely used by health organizations like the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to classify weight categories, it is important to know that different standards apply depending on age and ethnicity.

---

### 1. Standard BMI Categories for Adults (Ages 20+)
For most European, North American, and Caucasian populations, the standard WHO and CDC BMI classifications are:

| BMI Range (kg/m²) | Weight Status | Risk of Associated Health Issues |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Below 18.5** | Underweight | Minimal (but higher risk of nutritional deficiencies) |
| **18.5 to 24.9** | Healthy / Normal Weight | Low |
| **25.0 to 29.9** | Overweight | Increased |
| **30.0 to 34.9** | Obese (Class I / Low-risk) | High |
| **35.0 to 39.9** | Obese (Class II / Moderate-risk) | Very High |
| **40.0 and above** | Obese (Class III / Severe) | Extremely High |

---

### 2. Asian & South Asian BMI Standards
Research shows that Asian populations tend to accumulate more visceral fat (fat around abdominal organs) and have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease at lower BMIs than Caucasian populations. 

Because of this, the WHO Western Pacific Region and various Asian health ministries use a modified scale:

| BMI Range (kg/m²) | Weight Status (Asian Standard) | Risk of Metabolic Diseases |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Below 18.5** | Underweight | Increased risk of nutritional deficiencies |
| **18.5 to 22.9** | Healthy / Normal Weight | Low |
| **23.0 to 24.9** | Overweight (At Risk) | Moderate / Increasing |
| **25.0 to 27.4** | Obese (Class I) | High |
| **27.5 and above** | Obese (Class II / High Risk) | Very High |

*(Note: In China, the national standard classifies a BMI of **24.0 to 27.9** as overweight, and **28.0 or above** as obese.)*

---

### 3. How BMI is Calculated
BMI is calculated using one of two formulas, depending on the system of measurement:

* **Metric System:**
  $$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{Weight (kg)}}{\text{Height (m)}^2}$$

* **Imperial System:**
  $$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{Weight (lbs)}}{\text{Height (in)}^2} \times 703$$

---

### 4. BMI Categories for Children and Teens (Ages 2 to 19)
Because children are still growing and their body composition changes rapidly, their BMI is not evaluated using static numbers. Instead, it is plotted on a growth chart as a **percentile** relative to children of the same age and sex:

* **Underweight:** Below the 5th percentile
* **Healthy Weight:** 5th percentile to less than the 85th percentile
* **Overweight:** 85th percentile to less than the 95th percentile
* **Obese:** 95th percentile or higher
* **Severely Obese:** 120% of the 95th percentile or higher, or a BMI of 35+

---

### 5. Important Limitations of BMI
While BMI is a useful population screening tool, it has several major limitations when applied to individuals:
* **Muscle vs. Fat:** BMI only measures total mass relative to height. Because muscle is denser than fat, highly muscular individuals (like athletes or bodybuilders) can fall into the "overweight" or "obese" categories despite having low body fat.
* **Age:** Older adults naturally lose muscle mass (sarcopenia) and may have high body fat percentages even if their BMI is in the "healthy" range.
* **Fat Distribution:** BMI does not capture *where* you carry fat. Excess fat stored around the abdomen (visceral fat) is far more hazardous to health than fat stored around the hips and thighs. 

Because of these limitations, healthcare providers often look at BMI alongside other metrics, such as **waist circumference**, body fat percentage, and overall metabolic blood work (cholesterol, blood sugar, and blood pressure).
